articles.body:
Incumbent coalition Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) needs to win just 13 of the remaining 53 contested seats to secure a majority, with analysts describing the scale of the walkovers as “unprecedented”.

KUALA LUMPUR: Campaigning for Sarawak’s 13th state election kicked off on Saturday (Nov 28) with the incumbent Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) already tightening its grip on power before a single vote has even been cast.

The coalition, led by caretaker premier Abang Johari Openg, secured 29 of the 82 seats uncontested after nominations closed on Saturday.

This comes as major Peninsular Malaysia-based political parties and coalitions have chosen to sit out the polls, giving GPS a wide berth.

GPS now needs to win just 13 of the remaining 53 contested seats on Dec 12 to secure a simple majority in the state assembly.

The walkovers also mean that about 30 per cent of Sarawak’s over two million eligible voters, or 632,149 people, will not need to cast their ballots on polling day, the Election Commission said.

The polls marked a sharp contrast to the 2021 state election, when all 82 seats were contested, although GPS still cruised to a landslide victory then with 76 seats.

"UNPRECEDENTED"

Analysts told CNA that while the walkovers had been expected, the sheer scale of uncontested seats was unprecedented in Malaysian state elections.

“This is groundbreaking and unprecedented; it has never happened in any state in Malaysia. We can usually expect maybe five or six walkovers in Sarawak,” said Jayum Jawan of the Institute of Borneo Studies in Universiti Malaysia Sarawak.

“It is a great endorsement of Abang Johari’s leadership.”

Election Commission chairman Ramlan Harun said on Saturday that the 29 seats won uncontested marked the highest number in Sarawak state election history, surpassing the previous record of 19 seats in 1996, reported Malay Mail.

GPS fielded candidates in all 82 constituencies, including 11 new faces.

Among those who won unopposed were Abang Johari, who is also GPS chairman, his deputies Awang Tengah Ali Hasan and Douglas Uggah Embas, as well as GPS information chief Abdul Karim Rahman Hamzah.

“Even without a contest, it reflects the confidence that the people have placed in GPS all this while, and we will continue our efforts for the future of Sarawak,” Abang Johari said at a press conference, as quoted by Sarawak Tribune.

The caretaker premier retained his Gedong seat uncontested.

According to the Election Commission, the remaining 53 seats will see nine four-cornered contests, 15 three-cornered fights, and 29 straight fights.

A total of 168 candidates are contesting the election, compared with 349 back in 2021.

The Dec 12 polls - the fourth state election in Malaysia this year – come on the back of the ones earlier held in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka.

MAJOR PENINSULAR PARTIES SIT OUT POLLS

Of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, only the Democratic Action Party (DAP) is contesting the Sarawak state election, with Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) and Parti Amanah Negara (Amanah) sitting out.

DAP will contest 14 seats, down from 21 in the 2021 election, when it won two seats.

Other parties contesting include Parti Bansa Dayak Sarawak (PBDS) which will contest 29 seats, Parti Bumi Kenyalang with 17, Parti Bangsa Malaysia with three and Parti Aspirasi Rakyat Sawarak with one.

There are also 22 independent candidates, according to the Election Commission.

While GPS is widely expected to maintain its grip on power, its dominance could weaken political competition, analysts said.

“They should be able to win many of the other seats easily with landslides. I hope it is not a clean sweep. This would not be good for any democracy,” said Jayum, noting that many rural areas in the state still lacked basic infrastructure.

Jayun added that Malaysia's major political coalitions were reluctant to antagonise GPS, whose support could prove crucial in forming the next federal government.

Malaysia’s next general election must be held by February 2028.

“We should be looking at the bigger picture. How did Sarawak reach a point where the only truly contestable seats are in urban, Chinese-majority areas?” said James Chin, a professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.

Speaking to reporters on Saturday, GPS’ Abang Johari expressed his appreciation to parties in the federal unity government for their decision not to field candidates in the Borneo state, reported Sarawak Tribune.

The decision reflected the mutual understanding between the federal and Sarawak governments, he added.

Prior to the dissolution of the Sarawak legislative assembly, GPS held 79 seats, including three won by opposition lawmakers who later joined a GPS component party.

Two seats were held by DAP, while the remaining seat belonged to an independent.

PKR’s decision to sit out the polls drew ire from Sarawak DAP chairman Chong Chieng Jen, who questioned the move. Chong suggested that PKR was reluctant to contest to avoid jeopardising GPS’ support for the federal government.

But Anwar has denied that his party was “submitting” to GPS.

“It is cooperation, not submission,” the prime minister said on Nov 26, according to local media.

Ahead of nomination day, Barisan Nasional (BN) as well as component parties within the federal opposition Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition - Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS) and Parti Wawasan Negara (Wawasan) - also announced that they were sitting out the polls.

PN’s erstwhile component party - the Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu) - also confirmed its withdrawal.

Earlier this month, PAS secretary-general Takiyuddin Hassan said that the Islamist party decided to skip the Sarawak polls – which it has contested since 2001 - after weighing current political developments and “other considerations”.

It has never won a seat there before.

“PAS will remain committed to efforts to bolster unity, political stability and the people’s well-being, in line with the party’s principles and policies,” he said in a statement, as reported by local news outlet Free Malaysia Today.

Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi – who hails from BN and is president of the United Malaysia National Organisation (UMNO) – said that the coalition will not contest any seats in the 13th Sarawak state election.

“BN has no intention of contesting any state seats in Sarawak, as this is the understanding between UMNO and PBB in the state,” Zahid said, referring to the Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu, a lynchpin party of the GPS coalition.

The election comes as Sarawak pushes for greater autonomy within the Malaysian federation.

The Borneo state has been pushing for greater control over its own affairs and rights, including through its acquisition of an airline, its takeover of a port and a bank.

The Sarawak government is also seeking regulatory control over its oil and gas reserves through its wholly owned energy firm Petroleum Sarawak Bhd (Petros), posing a challenge to national oil corporation Petronas' monopoly over Malaysia’s lucrative hydrocarbon reserves.

articles.summary: La Finlandia affronta fallimenti, disoccupazione e una procedura europea per deficit eccessivo. Per risanare i conti pubblici il governo ha deciso di tagliare lo stato sociale, alimentando il malcontento

articles.body:
Secondo l’ufficio nazionale di statistica in Finlandia hanno dichiarato fallimento nell’ultimo anno 4.092 aziende. È il numero più alto dal 2000: nel solo mese di ottobre le imprese che hanno chiuso i battenti sono state 364, il 5 per cento in più rispetto allo stesso mese del 2025.

I fallimenti riguardano vari settori, dalla manifattura alla ristorazione fino ai trasporti, e sono un ulteriore segnale che in un paese considerato da nove anni il più felice del mondo, almeno secondo il World happiness report dell’università britannica di Oxford, c’è qualche problema di troppo.

Lo ha confermato anche il Fondo monetario internazionale, secondo il quale nel 2026 l’economia finlandese ha mostrato segni di ripresa, ma “la disoccupazione resta alta”. Il ministero degli affari economici stima che alla fine dell’anno il tasso di disoccupazione dovrebbe raggiungere il 10,3 per cento, prima di scendere gradualmente al 9,6 per cento nel 2027 e al 9,4 per cento tra due anni; all’inizio del 2026 era al 10,8 per cento, il tasso più alto dell’Unione europea.

L’Fmi ha raccomandato a Helsinki di concentrarsi sul risanamento dei conti pubblici, sull’eccessivo indebitamento delle famiglie e sul miglioramento del sistema scolastico.

L’economia finlandese, spiega Bloomberg, non è mai riuscita a riprendersi pienamente dai tempi della grandi crisi finanziaria globale del 2008 e soprattutto dal crollo della Nokia, che fino a una ventina d’anni fa rappresentava il 4 per cento del pil nazionale e quasi un quarto del gettito fiscale derivante dalle imposte sulle società.

Dal 2009 il debito pubblico è cresciuto senza sosta, in gran parte per finanziare la spesa pensionistica: la popolazione in età da lavoro si è ridotta con l’uscita della generazione del dopoguerra, che non è stata rimpiazzata da un numero sufficiente di immigrati. Ne hanno fatto le spese anche altri servizi essenziali, come la sanità e l’istruzione.

Con i debiti si è cercato di compensare il calo delle entrate provenienti dalle tasse del settore privato, che nel frattempo è sprofondato nella crisi. A quel punto il governo di Helsinki è caduto in un circolo vizioso: per contenere il debito pubblico ha dovuto tagliare la spesa sociale, indebolendo ulteriormente l’economia.

Così all’inizio del 2026 l’Unione europea ha deciso di aprire una procedura per deficit eccessivo sulla Finlandia, visto che il paese aveva chiuso il 2024 con un disavanzo di bilancio pari al 4,4 per cento del pil e il 2025 al 4,3 per cento. Helsinki dovrebbe rientrare sotto la soglia del 3 per cento entro il 2028, se vuole evitare “ammende o addirittura la sospensione dei finanziamenti comunitari”.

Preoccupati per il futuro

La notizia ha suscitato un particolare clamore in un paese spesso classificato tra i cosiddetti “stati frugali”, che hanno sempre guardato con disappunto ai paesi dell’Unione europea noti per il disordine dei loro conti pubblici. Tra questi c’è l’Italia, che oggi è sottoposta alla procedura per debito eccessivo proprio insieme alla Finlandia.

Di pari passo crescono anche i problemi politici: “I finlandesi sostengono il risanamento dei conti pubblici”, aggiunge Bloomberg, “ma i sondaggi mostrano una crescente insoddisfazione per il modo in cui sono stati attuati i tagli”.

Secondo un’indagine commissionata dal Finnish business and policy forum, il 52 per cento degli intervistati ritiene che le persone che dipendono dai sussidi siano state colpite in modo sproporzionato. Man mano che la rete di sicurezza sociale s’indebolisce, cresce la preoccupazione che nella società finlandese aumenti il divario tra ricchi e poveri. In sostanza, gli abitanti del paese più felice del mondo ora cominciano ad avere una visione del futuro piuttosto negativa.

Il pessimismo riguarda soprattutto il problema della disoccupazione. Di recente il quotidiano svizzero Neue Zürcher Zeitung ha pubblicato un reportage da Heinola, una cittadina di 18mila abitanti a due ore di auto da Helsinki, che descrive bene la situazione.

Qui la disoccupazione supera abbondantemente il 15 per cento. Dopo l’inizio della guerra in Ucraina, nel febbraio 2022, anche la Finlandia ha interrotto i legami commerciali con la Russia, penalizzando duramente i settori del legno e delle costruzioni, fondamentali per l’economia di Heinola. È così che nella cittadina molti non riescono più a trovare un impiego, mentre il costo della vita continua ad aumentare.

Di certo non c’è traccia dei centomila posti di lavoro promessi al momento dell’insediamento, tre anni fa, dal governo conservatore guidato da Petteri Orpo. Anzi: ora il governo ha annunciato un drastico giro di vite al tradizionale sistema di welfare finlandese.

Nel paese scandinavo lo stato si prende cura dei cittadini attraverso un’ampia gamma di prestazioni sociali che sono state continuamente rafforzate a partire dagli anni sessanta (oggi ci sono più di cento diverse forme di assistenza). Secondo Orpo, tutto questo costa troppo ed è arrivato il momento di far capire che “lavorare è più gratificante che ricevere sussidi”.

Incentivi e tagli

Il 1 settembre il governo ha presentato la legge finanziaria per il 2027, una proposta che prevede sgravi fiscali per incentivare il lavoro e le imprese, compensati da profondi tagli alle entrate per riequilibrare i conti. Dal 1 gennaio 2027, per esempio, l’aliquota minima dell’imposta sui redditi societari sarà ridotta al 18 per cento per favorire il lavoro autonomo, insieme a una tassazione più favorevole delle stock option dei dipendenti.

Allo stesso tempo saranno attuati tagli alla spesa per 4,8 miliardi di euro, che si aggiungeranno a quelli già decisi l’anno scorso: tra le proposte ci sono l’abolizione degli assegni familiari o quella di vari sussidi per fratelli e genitori single. Il ministero delle finanze, inoltre, vuole tagliare le prestazioni di sicurezza sociale, come l’indennità generale per l’alloggio.

Un’altra proposta significativa è l’adeguamento o lo smantellamento degli aumenti di spesa indicizzati, congelando gli adeguamenti al costo della vita almeno per un periodo.

Questi tagli si innestano nelle riforme varate l’anno scorso per convincere i finlandesi che, come dice il primo ministro Orpo, è meglio lavorare che ricevere sussidi. Nel 2026, in particolare, Helsinki ha stabilito che i cittadini senza lavoro hanno l’obbligo di iscriversi al registro dei disoccupati e di cercare un lavoro a tempo pieno, altrimenti gli altri sussidi sociali gli saranno ridotti (fino al 50 per cento).

Intanto a Heinola, racconta la Neue Zürcher Zeitung, Marta-Laura Treufeldt, 28 anni, ha risposto a quasi cento annunci di lavoro dopo aver preso la patente per guidare i camion, ma in dieci mesi è stata invitata a un colloquio solo una volta, ed è andata male. “Seduta al caffè della piazza centrale del paese dice che tutto questo è ‘abbastanza scoraggiante’”, scrive la Nzz.

Treufeldt prende un sussidio di 540 euro netti al mese, oltre a 260 euro per l’alloggio. Ma ha già ricevuto dall’ufficio del lavoro una lettera in cui si ricorda che bisogna candidarsi ad almeno un posto di lavoro al mese per evitare un taglio all’assegno sociale. ◆

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Economica.

articles.summary: Carolyn Marvin è diventata una sorta di celebrità a Filadelfia dopo aver deciso di dare battaglia a queste macchine, che ormai sono ovunque sui marciapiedi della città statunitense

articles.body:
A Filadelfia è una fresca mattina d’autunno. Nascosta in fondo a un vicolo piuttosto squallido, di fronte al garage della Patriot parking, Carolyn Marvin ci comunica le istruzioni per la missione antirobot a cui stiamo per partecipare. Una volta identificato il bersaglio, lo seguiremo fino a un marciapiede affollato. A quel punto Marvin, 78 anni, si metterà davanti al robot, impedendogli di avanzare. Il fotografo e io ci daremo il cambio per assicurarci che la polizia non ci porti tutti via.

Se Marvin dà l’impressione di avere già fatto qualcosa di simile, è perché è così. Lo ha già fatto diverse volte. Docente di comunicazione dell’università della Pennsylvania ormai quasi in pensione, è diventata una sorta di celebrità locale dopo aver deciso di dare battaglia ai robot di Uber Eats, una presenza fissa nel centro di Filadelfia. Marvin non entra in azione ogni giorno – “ho anche una vita privata” – ma quando lo fa si mette davanti al robot e lo fissa con aria di sfida. È una forma di protesta contro l’invasione delle macchine negli spazi pubblici.

Le sue iniziative sono diventate virali, al punto che per Halloween alcuni abitanti di Filadelfia si sono vestiti da “Marvin e il robot”. La professoressa può contare su tanti ammiratori, ma la sua protesta non è apprezzata da tutti. Qualche settimana fa è finita nei guai con la legge.

In arresto

“Stavo tornando a casa dopo aver fatto il vaccino contro l’influenza, quando ho visto un robot”, racconta. “Dato che avevo un po’ di tempo da perdere, mi ci sono piazzata davanti. Era in un punto molto trafficato”. Una folla si è immediatamente radunata attorno a lei, poi è nato un dibattito acceso. Alcuni dei presenti erano d’accordo con Marvin, secondo cui i robot per le consegne a domicilio, oltre a eliminare posti di lavoro, sono un pericolo per le persone con difficoltà motorie. A altri non piaceva che il suo intervento potesse impedire a un cliente di ricevere i piatti per cui aveva pagato. Alla fine qualcuno ha chiamato la polizia, riferendo che era in corso “un atto di vandalismo” contro un robot per le consegne. Sul posto sono arrivati tre agenti.

“Mi hanno chiesto di spostarmi. Ho risposto ‘No, il primo emendamento mi permette di protestare contro le multinazionali nello stesso spazio pubblico occupato dai robot’. Non c’era alcun motivo per cui dovessi allontanarmi”. Gli agenti, presumibilmente disorientati da quella figura minuta ma assolutamente determinata, con indosso la sua caratteristica visiera blu, hanno continuato a cercare di convincerla. Marvin non ha smesso di fissare il robot.

“Allora mi hanno presa, mi hanno tolto il cibo che avevo in mano, mi hanno ammanettata e mi hanno spinta verso la loro auto”, racconta Marvin. “Ho cercato di rendergli la vita difficile, ma erano tre contro una. Mentre mi portavano via ho continuato a discutere con loro. Penso che non fossero sicuri di potermi arrestare, perché la faccenda dei robot è nuova. Hanno esitato a lungo. Credo che il mio riferimento al primo emendamento gli sia apparso abbastanza sensato”.

Alla fine la polizia di Filadelfia ha multato Marvin per disturbo dell’ordine pubblico perché stava interrompendo un’attività commerciale. La donna è ancora in attesa di conoscere la data dell’udienza perché vuole contestare la multa. “Gli ingranaggi della giustizia si muovono lentamente, ma io mi presenterò in tribunale per esporre il mio punto di vista”, spiega.

Posso immaginare che le sue argomentazioni risulteranno piuttosto convincenti. Marvin ha scritto un libro molto apprezzato – When old technologies were new – sulle conseguenze dei mezzi di comunicazione sulla società. È una studiosa conosciuta. Nel 1985 è diventata la prima donna a ottenere un posto di ruolo alla Annenberg school for comunication dell’università della Pennsylvania, che ora le ha intitolato una cattedra.

L’attesa dell’udienza non ha rallentato l’azione di Marvin. Per questo oggi ha accettato che la accompagnassi nella sua missione antirobot. Ho scelto il luogo del nostro appuntamento dopo aver notato che lì si radunavano molte macchine in attesa degli ordini dei clienti. In questo modo avremmo potuto facilmente seguirli quando sarebbero partiti per le consegne.

La strategia delle aziende

Al momento non è chiaro quanti robot siano attivi a Filadelfia. La Avride, azienda con sede in Texas che produce le macchine, si è limitata a comunicarmi che il numero varia in base alla domanda. Siamo arrivati nel vicolo intorno all’ora del brunch e ne abbiamo trovati solo due.

Un robot mostra immagini di Halloween a intermittenza sullo schermo , mentre l’altro sfoggia la scritta “Zzz”, come se stesse dormendo. Devo ammettere che il loro aspetto è carino. Naturalmente si tratta di una scelta precisa. “Umanizzare i robot è importante, perché sono una presenza del tutto nuova”, mi ha spiegato un portavoce della Avride quando ho chiamato l’azienda per chiedere un’intervista, un paio di giorni fa. “Vogliamo che le persone si sentano a proprio agio, non che abbiano paura di una scatola inquietante che cammina sul marciapiede”.

L’umanizzazione non ha ingannato Marvin, ma con altre persone sembra funzionare. La Avride, che gestisce quasi mille macchine per la consegna di cibo in più di 25 diversi campus universitari e in un numero crescente di città, come Jersey City e Austin, riferisce che in passato riceveva email preoccupate dalle persone che avevano visto un robot in standby e presumevano che si fosse perso o fosse guasto. Per questo motivo gli ingegneri hanno aggiunto la scritta “zzz” sullo schermo, in modo da far capire che l’apparecchio era in attesa di ricevere un ordine. A quel punto le email si sono interrotte. Ho chiesto al portavoce della Avride se avesse sentito parlare di Carolyn Marvin. Ha taciuto per un attimo, poi ha risposto: “Conosciamo perfettamente questa signora, sì”.

Mentre aspettiamo che i robot si mettano in moto, mi domando se la notorietà della professoressa possa aver spinto la Avride a creare una “modalità Marvin” per bloccare le macchine quando rilevano la sua presenza. Aspettiamo da circa quaranta minuti e ancora non succede nulla. Finalmente, dopo un segnale acustico, un robot si attiva. Qualcuno ha inoltrato un ordine e l’apparecchio numero 1617 si dirige verso un ristorante vicino per ritirare il cibo da consegnare.

Anche se è dotato di telecamere, sensori e un software basato sull’intelligenza artificiale (ia), il povero robot non ha l’istinto necessario per capire che la sua missione sta per essere bloccata. Lo seguiamo lungo il vicolo. Appena imbocca Walnut street, una delle strade principali del centro, Marvin gli si mette davanti e gli impedisce di proseguire.

Per qualche minuto i passanti ignorano il faccia a faccia tra la professoressa e la macchina, anche se mi accorgo che una donna passa accanto a noi alzando gli occhi in segno d’insofferenza. Poi arrivano i complimenti e le domande. Una signora anziana ringrazia calorosamente Marvin. Un uomo di mezza età in abiti eleganti la incoraggia: “Qualcuno deve pur farlo!”. Un altro passante dice di apprezzare lo sforzo di Marvin e dice: “La gig economy è uno schifo per tutti!”.

“Oh mio dio!”, esclama una ragazza di nome Cadence quando riconosce Marvin e la sua visiera blu. “È una leggenda! Mi sembra di aver incontrato una celebrità!”. Cadence, 22 anni, appena laureata, sostiene la protesta della professoressa. “L’intelligenza artificiale e la robotica dovrebbero renderci la vita più semplice e aiutarci a fare le cose che ci piacciono, non rubare il lavoro alla gente”, sottolinea. “Cerco di aiutare le piccole attività commerciali che non usano l’ia”.

Alcuni ragazzini, più che preoccuparsi della gig economy, sono interessati alle facce accattivanti dei robot. Tutti i bambini indicano gli apparecchi e sorridono. Una coppia di giovani comincia una discussione animata per stabilire se il robot somigli più a un cane o a un gatto (in realtà non somiglia né a un cane né a un gatto). L’unico bambino che non mostra minimamente di essere affascinato dalla macchina sembra avere circa sette anni e urla: “Rottame!”. Poi aggiunge: “Ho visto abbastanza film da sapere che questi cosi ci daranno la caccia”.

Il sostegno a Marvin non è un caso isolato. Le proteste della donna convincono perché si ricollegano a una sfiducia totale nei confronti dell’ia e dell’automazione. Secondo uno studio recente del Pew research center, la maggioranza degli statunitensi è profondamente scettica nei confronti dell’intelligenza artificiale. Gli adulti convinti che questa tecnologia avrà effetti negativi sono la maggioranza. Non sono sicuro che oggi ci sia qualcun altro che blocchi i robot per le consegne, ma è innegabile che le proteste contro i data center e altri simboli dell’automazione siano in forte crescita.

Alcune settimane fa a Filadelfia ho incrociato una donna che stava in piedi davanti a un taxi a guida autonoma della Waymo, in fase di sperimentazione in città (con a bordo autisti umani per garantire la sicurezza). La donna impediva al veicolo di proseguire e gli urlava: “Sfigato!”.

Eppure, nonostante questa antipatia diffusa, i robot stanno entrando nella vita quotidiana degli statunitensi. La Pennsylvania ha legalizzato quelli per le consegne con l’Act 106 del 2020, attribuendogli lo status di “pedoni”. Oggi fanno parte del paesaggio urbano.

Quando gli apparecchi della Arvide sono apparsi per la prima volta a Filadelfia, lo scorso marzo, la gente li fissava sorpresa e si scattava delle foto con loro. Oggi, invece, quasi tutti li ignorano. Lo stesso fenomeno si sta verificando in altre città del mondo. Anche se non è chiaro quanti robot per la consegna di cibo siano in attività a livello globale, sappiamo che negli Stati Uniti esistono diverse aziende come la Avride. Una delle più grandi è la Serve Robotics, con una flotta di circa duemila robot.

A prescindere dai grandi piani di espansione dell’industria dell’automazione, Marvin continua a protestare perché vuole ricordare agli statunitensi che hanno il diritto di esprimersi su questo sviluppo e di stabilire se i robot delle aziende private debbano avere il permesso di occupare le strade pubbliche.

“Sono molto felice dei passi avanti in campo medico dovuti all’intelligenza artificiale”, sottolinea Marvin. “Inoltre penso che i robot vadano benissimo nelle fabbriche. Ma non devono occupare gli spazi pubblici. Non credo che tutto questo sia inevitabile, ma ci vuole la volontà di cambiare le cose. A Toronto hanno bandito dai marciapiedi i robot per le consegne già nel 2021. Penso che la domanda sia semplice: a chi devono servire le infrastrutture pubbliche?”.

Il robot che si trova davanti a Marvin non è (ancora) abbastanza intelligente da rispondere a questa domanda, ma sembra aver capito che oggi non riuscirà a raggiungere il ristorante e ritirare il cibo per la consegna. Dopo aver ripetutamente cercato di aggirare la professoressa, sembra rassegnarsi a entrare in standby. Alla fine Marvin, che deve andare al campus per preparare una lezione, si fa da parte. Il robot si rianima immediatamente e rientra nel garage. So bene che è soltanto un computer su ruote, ma potrei giurare che è demoralizzato. Marvin, invece, ha un’espressione trionfante.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

articles.body:
Rafael Grossi, director general del Organismo Internacional de Energía Atómica (OIEA), ha elegido a Alexei Ferapontov, un alto cargo de la órbita del presidente ruso, Vladímir Putin, para dirigir el Departamento de Energía Nuclear de la agencia de la ONU. Esta decisión ha provocado malestar en Ucrania y en la Unión Europea porque Ferapontov, que actualmente es un técnico veterano en la supervisión estatal de la energía en Rusia, donde se ocupa de la seguridad nuclear y radiológica, fue sancionado por Ucrania en 2023 por participar, según Kiev, en acciones para “legitimar la toma ilegal de la central nuclear de Zaporiyia ”.

articles.title: Guardare il calcio in tv è sempre più complicato e costoso
articles.summary: Il sistema dei diritti di trasmissione dei campionati più seguiti è talmente frammentato che gli appassionati devono avere vari abbonamenti contemporaneamente
articles.preview: Nella prossima serata di Champions league si giocheranno nove partite. Milioni di tifosi le vedranno, alcuni attraverso i servizi di streaming a pagamento e altri sui siti illegali. In un modo o nell’altro, guardare le partite di calcio sta diventando sempre più complicato. Se seguite la competizione > Champions league da qualche anno, probabilmente ricorderete un tempo in cui guardare le partite era molto più facile.
articles.body:
Nella prossima serata di Champions league si giocheranno nove partite. Milioni di tifosi le vedranno, alcuni attraverso i servizi di streaming a pagamento e altri sui siti illegali. In un modo o nell’altro, guardare le partite di calcio sta diventando sempre più complicato.

Se seguite la competizione > Champions league da qualche anno, probabilmente ricorderete un tempo in cui guardare le partite era molto più facile. Le emittenti nazionali e le aziende di telecomunicazioni spesso detenevano i diritti di trasmissione del calcio e includevano le partite nei loro pacchetti tv, internet e telefonici.

Quel modello sta cambiando, spiega Thomas Peeters, economista dello sport e docente della Erasmus school of economics, nei Paesi Bassi: “Molti dei diritti di trasmissione che un tempo erano in chiaro su uno dei canali disponibili sono stati divisi tra più servizi di streaming che si occupano specificamente di sport”.

In Germania, per esempio, Dazn trasmette tutte le partite di Champions league tranne quella più importante del martedì sera, di cui Prime Video ha l’esclusiva. In Italia è Sky a trasmettere la maggior parte delle partite, mentre Prime Video ha i diritti della partita di punta del mercoledì. Anche le principali piattaforme di streaming statunitensi stanno entrando nel mercato, con Disney+ e Paramount+ che faranno il loro esordio nella stagione 2027-2028.

Questi giganti dello streaming, con enormi risorse finanziarie, fanno concorrenza alle emittenti tradizionali e stanno facendo lievitare il prezzo dei diritti calcistici.

È una buona notizia per la Uefa, che li vende al miglior offerente: il valore dei diritti di trasmissione della Champions league nei cinque principali mercati europei (Regno Unito, Germania, Italia, Spagna e Francia) aumenterà di più del 20 per cento dal 2027.

Ma è una brutta notizia per gli spettatori. Se da un lato i contratti televisivi più vantaggiosi garantiscono maggiori entrate ai club, dall’altro comportano dei rischi finanziari per le emittenti, che potrebbero cercare di compensare aumentando i prezzi degli abbonamenti. Inoltre, se aumentano gli offerenti significa che i tifosi dovranno sottoscrivere più abbonamenti per seguire le partite.

Abbiamo fatto un po’ di conti. Nel Regno Unito per guardare la Premier league e la Champions league bisogna abbonarsi a Sky, Tnt Sports e Amazon Prime Video, per un costo totale di circa 826 sterline all’anno. In Germania per la Bundesliga e la Champions league bisogna avere Dazn, Sky e Amazon Prime Video, per un totale di circa 870 euro.

E stiamo parlando solo di due competizioni. Se aggiungiamo anche le altre, la spesa sfugge rapidamente di mano. In Spagna negli ultimi dieci anni il costo per guardare le partite di calcio è aumentato di quasi il 66 per cento. Nel Regno Unito, tra il 2019-2020 e il 2024-2025, seguire le quindici competizioni più popolari è diventato più costoso del 57 per cento.

Ma non tutti sono disposti a pagare. Nelle serate di Champions league, molti tifosi guardano le partite gratis, cioè in modo illegale.

Da uno studio condotto nel 2023 dall’ufficio dell’Unione europea per la proprietà intellettuale (Euipo) è emerso che nell’anno precedente il 12 per cento dei cittadini dell’Unione aveva guardato eventi sportivi in streaming su siti illegali. Tra le persone di età compresa tra i 15 e i 24 anni, la percentuale saliva al 27 per cento.

Guardare le partite sui siti illegali, però, non sempre è un’esperienza piacevole: lo streaming può bloccarsi, subire ritardi o improvvisi cali di qualità, ed è pieno di annunci pop-up di casinò online e pornografia.

Ma quei siti non sono più l’unica opzione. Un modello più organizzato, con abbonamento, è ormai diventato un elemento importante del mondo della pirateria: i servizi Iptv (Internet protocol television) illeciti che trasmettono programmi tv su internet senza l’autorizzazione dei titolari dei diritti.

I servizi Iptv offrono migliaia di canali, compresi quelli sportivi premium, per circa 75 euro all’anno, secondo l’organizzazione europea Audiovisual anti-piracy alliance (Aapa). La cifra è solo una frazione del prezzo degli abbonamenti legali. Gli utenti ottengono streaming stabile, buona qualità dell’immagine e perfino assistenza tramite WhatsApp.

Malware e furti di dati

Secondo le stime dell’Aapa, l’anno scorso 34,4 milioni di persone nell’Unione europea, nel Regno Unito e in Svizzera hanno usato i servizi Iptv illegali, circa il doppio rispetto al 2021.

Ma questi servizi comportano dei rischi. Secondo Eurojust, l’agenzia dell’Unione europea per la cooperazione giudiziaria penale, gli utenti possono essere esposti a malware e furti di dati, mentre i profitti dei fornitori possono “alimentare altre forme di criminalità organizzata, tra cui frodi, corruzione e traffico di droga”.

Gli utenti non sono al sicuro neanche dal punto di vista legale. Nel 2025 le autorità italiane hanno multato 2.266 utenti dei servizi di streaming illegali, infliggendo sanzioni dai 154 euro in su.

Tuttavia, la maggior parte delle azioni di contrasto si concentra sulle reti criminali che gestiscono i servizi piuttosto che sugli appassionati che guardano le partite dal divano di casa.

Un problema nel lungo periodo

Chi vuole guardare le partite troverà sempre un modo per farlo, ma uno degli aspetti positivi del vecchio modello era che i telespettatori potevano imbattersi in una partita di calcio facendo zapping. A guardare le partite, quindi, non erano solo gli appassionati.

Perdere tutti quei potenziali spettatori potrebbe diventare un problema per il calcio nel lungo periodo, secondo Peeters, convinto che debba continuare a conquistare le nuove generazioni, non limitarsi a spremere più soldi dai tifosi esistenti. “Le nuove generazioni devono poter vivere a fondo l’esperienza calcistica, capire cosa significa davvero essere tifoso di una squadra”, spiega. È più difficile farlo quando le partite finiscono sempre più spesso dietro un paywall.

Invertire la tendenza è molto difficile. Oggi molti dei più grandi eventi sportivi, tra cui i Mondiali, gli Europei e, in alcuni paesi, la finale di Champions league e la finale della coppa nazionale, sono protetti da norme per garantirne la disponibilità in tv in chiaro.

Ampliare queste tutele si sta però rivelando complicato. A giugno il parlamento francese ha respinto una proposta per garantire la visione gratuita di una partita del campionato nazionale a settimana, dopo che la lega calcio aveva avvertito che questo avrebbe ridotto il valore dei diritti televisivi, che rappresentano più del 50 per cento delle entrate dei club. I deputati britannici avevano respinto una proposta simile nel 2025.

Le cose vanno più spesso nella direzione opposta. Quest’anno nel Regno Unito la finale di Champions league è stata accessibile solo a pagamento per la prima volta dal 1992. Secondo un’analisi condotta per il quotidiano The Guardian, lo streaming illegale della partita avrebbe coinvolto 3,7 milioni di indirizzi Ip, rispetto alle sette milioni di persone che hanno visto la partita legalmente.

Se non volete pagare per vedere in streaming il prossimo turno di Champions league, chiamate un amico e andate a guardare la partita al pub. Forse è proprio questo il modo migliore per seguire il calcio. ◆

articles.body:
Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.

Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer MahiroÄlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.

MahiroÄlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.

In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.

Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator KÃ¼rÅad OÄuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.

MahiroÄlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.

"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.

The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip ErdoÄan and his administration.

The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.

ErdoÄan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.

However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.

Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.

ErdoÄan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem ImamoÄlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied.

Hundreds of ImamoÄlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

articles.title: Seoul monitoring signs of possible visit to China by North Korea’s Kim
articles.summary: Chinese leader Xi Jinping reportedly told South Korean President Lee Jae Myung during their summit earlier this month that Kim could visit China.
articles.preview: Seoul – South Korea’s spy agency said Saturday it was monitoring “various developments” about a possible visit to China by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, following reports on such a trip. China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a vital source of diplomatic, economic and political support for Pyongyang, although ties have not always been smooth.
articles.body:
Seoul – South Korea’s spy agency said Saturday it was monitoring “various developments” about a possible visit to China by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, following reports on such a trip.

China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a vital source of diplomatic, economic and political support for Pyongyang, although ties have not always been smooth.

Kim made an unannounced, one-day visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong in October, crossing a major bridge linking China and nuclear-armed North Korea that is widely considered a symbol of their deepening economic ties.

A South Korean broadcaster KBS, citing an unnamed diplomatic source, reported that Chinese leader Xi Jinping told his South Korean counterpart, Lee Jae Myung, during their summit earlier this month that Kim could visit China.

Citing an unnamed government source, it also reported that an “emergency order” had been issued in the Chinese border city of Dandong, echoing arrangements made for Kim’s October visit.

Seoul’s spy agency said Saturday it was “keeping a close eye on various developments,” when asked about the report.

Seoul’s presidential office said Xi did not mention what was described by the KBS report, adding that the administration “is closely monitoring developments in North Korea-China relations.”

Despite long-running U.N. sanctions, North Korea has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law, with its regime repeatedly declaring its atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible.

Kim has ignored repeated overtures for talks from U.S. President Donald Trump.

Experts say Pyongyang is effectively demanding U.S. recognition as a nuclear-armed state as a precondition for talks — a concession they say would pose complex diplomatic and security challenges for Washington, a key ally of Seoul.

A visit to China could give Kim an opportunity to discuss with Xi the outcome of the recent U.S.-China talks and trilateral summit involving Russia, another key ally of Pyongyang, experts say.

articles.body:
Washington – The U.S. military on Friday announced that it had disabled a Palau-flagged ship violating Washington’s blockade of Iranian ports.

Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, said an American aircraft had fired “precision munitions” on Thursday into the Pacific Archer’s stern after it attempted to run the blockade.

“The ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed,” the statement said, noting the incident occurred in the Gulf of Oman.

The Pacific Archer had left Bandar Abbas, an Iranian port on the Strait of Hormuz, the statement said.

CENTCOM said it “continues to strictly enforce the blockade,” which has seen six ships disabled and 158 others redirected.

The United States launched its blockade in mid-July following the collapse of a short-lived agreement with Iran.

Iran has meanwhile sought to impose its own blockade on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian forces have made multiple announcements in recent weeks of ships catching fire attempting to use routes that Tehran considers off-limits.

On Monday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei vowed to use all means at the country’s disposal to counter the U.S. blockade.

Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis — which broke out in late February with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran — remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June deal that laid out a pathway to a permanent settlement.

Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days but only if Washington agreed to its list of demands which include the lifting of the blockade.

articles.body:
Taiwan headed to the polls Saturday for local elections that could reshape the political field ahead of the 2028 presidential contest, with voters galvanized by an unexpectedly close race in the capital Taipei.

Some 19.6 million people are eligible to vote for mayors and county chiefs across 22 cities and counties, with more than 11,000 smaller roles up for grabs. Polls run from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., with initial results expected in the evening.

The vote will test whether President Lai Ching-te’s Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) can translate its record run of three straight presidential victories into gains at the local level, where the opposition Kuomintang (KMT) has long been stronger. For the KMT, which advocates friendlier ties with China, the results could reorder the field of politicians vying to challenge Lai in 2028 — a contest Beijing is closely watching.

articles.title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
articles.summary: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
articles.preview: Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment. Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support. But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis. This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.
articles.body:
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.

Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.

But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.

This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.

At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.

But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.

Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.

"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.

If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable â and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.

Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.

Barred from jobs

Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.

When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.

Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.

Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.

What is an ADHD or autism reassessment?

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.

"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.

The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.

Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.

But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.

"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.

"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."

Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.

During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".

'I was stuck'

Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.

"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."

It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.

"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.

"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.

The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.

"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."

In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.

Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.

Fears about stigma

The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.

"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.

Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.

Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.

Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.

'Magic spell'

People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.

Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".

"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.

Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.

Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.

The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.

"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.

Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.

She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.

"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

articles.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
articles.preview: For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar. "Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500." It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang.
articles.body:
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.

The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.

China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.

"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.

This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.

That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.

"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.

Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".

The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."

Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.

"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.

These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.

In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.

The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.

"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.

Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.

"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.

"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."

When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".

"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.

"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."

These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.

Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."

The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.

"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns: dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiananmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after. More recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.

Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."

But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".

"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.

For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.

Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.

The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.

In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.

"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked.

"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand."

The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says.

He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution."

* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

articles.title: 'Nobody is going to help us': India's drone and robotics firms face hurdles amid growing military demand
articles.summary: Border tensions and government support are driving India's drone and robotics manufacturers towards defence applications. But experts warn that reliance on imported components and unpredictable military orders could hinder long-term growth.
articles.preview: Border tensions and government support are driving India's drone and robotics manufacturers towards defence applications. But experts warn that reliance on imported components and unpredictable military orders could hinder long-term growth. BENGALURU: Three four-legged robots raced around a specially designed track at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, drawing crowds as they competed to clock the fastest lap. Param, developed by Bengaluru-based General Autonomy, won the race.
articles.body:
Border tensions and government support are driving India's drone and robotics manufacturers towards defence applications. But experts warn that reliance on imported components and unpredictable military orders could hinder long-term growth.

BENGALURU: Three four-legged robots raced around a specially designed track at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, drawing crowds as they competed to clock the fastest lap.

Param, developed by Bengaluru-based General Autonomy, won the race. But for the company's co-founder Farid Ahsan, the real test lies far from the racetrack - on the military front line.

“What is more hazardous than the job of a soldier on the front lines?” he asked rhetorically.

General Autonomy, which began in industrial automation, is now working with the Indian armed forces to explore military applications for its robotic dogs and humanoids, including surveillance, patrolling and transporting supplies.

It was among several manufacturers showcasing unmanned technologies at the three-day summit from Nov 17 to 19, as India's drone and robotics firms look to tap growing demand from the country’s defence sector.

“The defence market is so big, with orders running into billions of rupees. The projected demand is also extremely high, and it's kind of engulfing the civil market,” Ezhilan Nanmaran, head of product and strategic alliances at Indian drone manufacturer IdeaForge, told CNA.

In August 2026, India's Ministry of Defence signed contracts worth approximately 15.8 billion Indian rupees (US$170 million) with Indian manufacturers Tata Advanced Systems and NIBE for armed drones and related equipment for the Indian Army.

IdeaForge itself secured a 1.37-billion-rupee contract from the ministry in June 2025 to supply the Indian Army with small surveillance drones and accessories, according to its stock-exchange filing.

But industry players told CNA that turning growing demand into a sustainable business will depend on developing reliable technology, reducing reliance on imported components and securing a steady flow of orders.

DEFENCE DEMAND DRIVES INDIA'S DRONE BOOM

The Indian government is pushing to boost domestic defence manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers.

“India must work in a mission mode to emerge as a global hub of indigenous drone manufacturing in the next few years,” Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said at an industry conclave in New Delhi on Mar 19.

To support innovation, the government has introduced funding schemes including Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) and Acing Development of Innovative Technologies with iDEX (ADITI), which offers eligible startups grants of up to 250 million rupees each.

The number of new Indian companies founded in the defence-drone sector more than tripled from eight in 2022 to 26 in 2025, with another 33 established in the first 11 months of 2026, according to data from market intelligence firm Tracxn.

Drone manufacturers are increasingly focusing on defence applications over civilian uses such as urban deliveries, where commercial adoption remains limited, analysts said.

Neil Shah, vice-president of research at Counterpoint Research, said India's low-cost motorcycle deliveries, restrictions on long-distance drone flights and lack of landing infrastructure hinder commercial adoption.

“Covering the last mile is very tough in India,” he said. He added that drones were better suited to transporting goods between fixed locations, particularly for time-sensitive deliveries such as medical samples.

By contrast, growing military requirements and government support has created a stronger market for defence manufacturers, according to Shweta Rajpal Kohli, president and CEO of Startup Policy Forum, an Indian startup advocacy group.

“Geopolitics created the urgency. Policy created the suppliers,” she told CNA, referring to changing security priorities and government initiatives that have helped startups develop technologies for the armed forces.

“We would like to get into it (civilian drone applications), but right now we have good traction with police forces and army, so that's where our focus is at,” said Arjun Naga Vinay, assistant sales manager at Bengaluru-based drone firm NeoSky.

The company develops surveillance and mapping drones and is owned by Indian conglomerate RattanIndia Enterprises.

Vinay told CNA that the company had supplied 60 surveillance drones to Karnataka Police and subsequently received a repeat order. It has also trained around 150 policewomen to operate drones.

NeoSky is also helping Indian Army units establish drone-training facilities, providing equipment, simulators and training in drone assembly, maintenance and operation.

Meanwhile, General Autonomy's Farid Ahsan said heightened regional security tensions along India’s border with Pakistan last year prompted the company to shift from industrial automation to defence.

“We understood that the biggest requirement for adopting robotics in India is at the front line,” he said, citing the harsh conditions and risks faced by soldiers.

The company is exploring military applications for its robots with the Indian armed forces, although the machines remain under development and have yet to enter operational service.

HOW DRONES ARE RESHAPING MODERN WARFARE

Drones have become increasingly important in modern warfare, with conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East demonstrating their ability to carry out surveillance, strike targets and challenge traditional military defences.

The Russia-Ukraine war has been a turning point. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, both sides have deployed large numbers of drones to track enemy movements, direct artillery fire and strike troops, tanks and critical military and civilian infrastructure.

Relatively inexpensive drones have also allowed Ukrainian forces to strike Russian targets without relying solely on costly missiles or conventional aircraft. According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, drones had overtaken artillery as the leading cause of front-line casualties by 2025, accounting for up to 80 per cent of losses.

In the Middle East, Israel has used drones for surveillance and strikes in Gaza, while Iran has deployed explosive-laden drones against Israel and other targets in the region.

Iranian-designed Shahed drones - also used extensively by Russia in Ukraine - have demonstrated how large numbers of relatively cheap unmanned aircraft can overwhelm air defences and force opponents to expend costly interceptor missiles.

These conflicts have prompted governments worldwide to step up investment in military drones.

In February, Germany approved an initial 540 million euro order for attack drones, according to a Reuters report. While the US has earmarked US$1 billion to acquire about 340,000 small military drones over two years.

The United Kingdom announced plans in June 2025 to invest more than 4 billion pounds in autonomous military systems, including drones. In June 2026, it also pledged to supply Ukraine with 150,000 drones as part of a broader 752 million pound military aid package, according to its Ministry of Defence.

The surge in spending is creating opportunities for defence manufacturers, although rapidly evolving battlefield threats mean they must continually develop systems capable of resisting electronic interference and other countermeasures.

INDIA'S DRONE MAKERS PREPARE FOR TOUGHER MISSIONS

As India's military needs evolve, drone manufacturers are developing more advanced systems capable of operating in increasingly hostile environments.

IdeaForge's Nanmaran said India's border conflicts with Pakistan and China had highlighted the need for drones capable of withstanding electronic jamming and GPS spoofing - techniques used to disrupt communications and manipulate navigation systems.

“Flying a drone on your own border, looking at your border, is very different from flying in a contested environment,” he said.

Drone companies are also exploring applications beyond surveillance.

IdeaForge is developing a drone called Yeti to transport heavy supplies to remote areas.

Meanwhile, General Autonomy is exploring how four-legged robots and humanoids could patrol military installations, inspect hazardous areas and carry supplies across difficult terrain.

Ahsan said the company was adapting its machines to India's challenging geographical terrain, including mountainous regions, deserts and forests, where equipment developed for other countries might not be suitable.

But he acknowledged that this technology was still at an early stage.

Experience developing drones and robots for India's diverse terrain could also help manufacturers expand into overseas markets with similar conditions.

For instance, IdeaForge has used its drones for high-altitude mapping in the Himalayas and demonstrated their ability to operate in Alaska's freezing conditions to US defence customers, according to its FY2023-24 annual report.

The United States is among IdeaForge's priority overseas markets. The company said in its annual report that it had secured its first US order from a police department in Texas and formed a partnership to explore opportunities in Japan.

'NOBODY IS GOING TO HELP US WHEN THE CHIPS ARE DOWN'

Despite growing military demand, India's drone industry faces challenges including reliance on imported components and difficulties deploying new technologies, said experts.

Hari Kumar R, director of research and development at state-owned Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL), said India had made progress in developing electronic components domestically, but advanced infrared sensors used for night-time military surveillance remained difficult to source.

Speaking at a panel discussion at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, he stressed the need to develop local alternatives and diversify suppliers to prevent disruptions caused by shortages or foreign restrictions.

“Nobody is going to help us when the chips are down. Each country stands up to itself,” he said.

B.K. Das, a senior official at India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), also flagged reliance on imported materials, including rare earth magnets used in drone motors.

“[The challenge is] we do research in isolation,” he told CNA, calling for greater collaboration among India's research institutions, startups and defence companies to develop advanced military systems.

Das said DRDO had established 15 centres at universities and research institutions to help bridge that gap.

Das acknowledged that emerging technologies still needed further development to meet stringent military standards, including the ability to withstand harsh weather, equipment failures and other challenging conditions.

Meanwhile, securing a predictable flow of military orders remains another challenge for Indian startups operating in the space.

Citing Ministry of Defence figures, Kohli said 45 procurement contracts worth about 23.3 billion Indian rupees had been signed under the government's iDEX initiative as of February.

“Revenue is real now, but much of it is still lumpy,” Kohli said, referring to the irregular flow of orders and income for defence startups.

She said emergency military purchases had helped some companies secure business, but sporadic orders made it difficult for startups to plan long-term investments, expand production and retain skilled workers.

“A startup cannot hire engineers or build a factory on orders that arrive in bursts,” she said.

Kohli added that more predictable procurement, stronger domestic supply chains and manufacturing capabilities would be key to building a sustainable defence-tech industry in India.

“The market becomes sustainable when one-time buys turn into multi-year orders,” she said.
