articles.preview: Hundreds of thousands of Canadians call for Pete Hoekstra to be declared ‘persona non grata’ A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries. Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party member, originally opened the petition for signatures in July 2026 after a woman from Calgary sponsored it.
articles.body:
A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries.

Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party member, originally opened the petition for signatures in July 2026 after a woman from Calgary sponsored it. The petition requests that the Canadian government declare Hoekstra “persona non grata” due to his “US” diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs”.

“He has been repeatedly abusive and insulting to Canadians,” May said as she formally introduced the petition, according to Politico.

She called Donald Trump’s envoy “the most undiplomatic diplomat” Canada had ever seen.

The petition accuses Hoekstra of “undermining” Canada-US diplomatic relations through repeated statements about Canadian politics that its signatories say are “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol”.

The US state department said it was aware of the petition.

Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particularly for his response to Trump’s desire to annex the country and make Canada the 51st US state.

Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the president’s rhetoric as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”.

Hoekstra also previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election that saw a remarkable come-from-behind victory for the prime minister’s Liberal party as “anti-American”.

The US ambassador had suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans performed poorly in this month’s midterm elections.

“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” Carney replied, when asked about the comments.

Democrats swept the November elections, including key Senate races in border states such as Michigan and Maine, where the bitter tariff war between Washington and Ottawa has hit residents hard.

Last month Carney said American tariffs hurt both American and Canadian households. He added that auto exports to the US had so far fallen 10%, and US exports to Canada have fallen by more than 20%.

“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”

Hoekstra had also accused Canada of potential “political interference” in the US election, a claim Carney said held “no merit”. Speaking to reporters in Turkey, the prime minister said he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.

Even though the Canadian government is required to provide a formal response to the petition presented by May, the petition is nonbinding.

“I think the government will quite likely say, ‘No, we’re not prepared to declare Pete Hoekstra persona non grata and strip him of his diplomatic credentials,’”, May said in an interview with CTV.

Despite this possibility, May expects the petition to signal to Trump that the Canadian government has the support of its constituents, and she hopes the government can use it as leverage against Trump with Democrats holding power in Congress for the second half of Trump’s term.

articles.title: Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill
articles.summary: Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.
articles.preview: November 27, 2026 Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights. Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants. However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.
articles.body:
November 27, 2026

Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.

However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.

Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.

Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

What did the Supreme Court say about the law?

Chief Justice Richard Wagner said that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society."

Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.

"This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.

CAQ ruled Quebec in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.

Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

Critics argue secularism bill weakens rights protections

Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

"This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.

Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy."

articles.title: UKMTO says five percent of ships attacked since 17 Aug sunk or lost
articles.summary: UKMTO says five percent of ships attacked since 17 Aug sunk or lost About 5 percent of vessels reported attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz have been confirmed lost or sunk since the Iran-US Memorandum of Understanding expired on 17 August, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). Roughly 43 percent of ships in these incidents appear on the non-compliance list of the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA), which was set up by Iran in May, UKMTO said in its weekly overview. The PGSA blacklists ships it accuses of breaking its Hormuz transit rules, threatening fines, detention or confiscation. Its list passed 120 vessels in October. According to the weekly overview, three tankers were struck by unknown projectiles within about 17 minutes on 22 November while heading east through the Strait of Hormuz. All three continued their voyages. UKMTO documented 10 incidents in the week to 25 November, seven of them in the Strait of Hormuz. Combined transits remain roughly 65 percent below pre-conflict levels, with 166 outbound and 173 inbound crossings last week. About 70 percent were energy carriers, and more vessels are using the southern route.

articles.body:
Ucrania lleva la legítima defensa ante Rusia al Báltico y el Mediterráneo, pero las operaciones requieren el maximo cuidado

Ucrania ha llevado la defensa contra Rusia más allá de sus fronteras, con ataques y sabotajes en aguas europeas contra barcos rusos, sean militares o de transporte marítimo. Kiev ha ampliado esta semana su radio de castigo hasta golpear una corbeta rusa en la costa de Libia, en el Mediterráneo. Días atrás, un dron ucranio impactó contra un carguero ruso en aguas internacionales del mar Báltico. El barco navegó ardiendo a la deriva en dirección a Finlandia y puso en estado de alerta a uno de los aliados más fieles de la causa ucrania, especialmente sensibilizado por su vecindad con Rusia.

No es la primera vez que la guerra se amplía hasta el Mediterráneo. La primera operación de este tipo confirmada por Kiev se desarrolló en diciembre de 2025. En aquel episodio, dos drones náuticos destruyeron el petrolero Qendil en aguas internacionales entre Malta y Grecia. El Qendil era un buque de la llamada “flota fantasma”, navíos que sirven a Rusia para saltarse las sanciones occidentales sobre sus exportaciones.

En marzo de 2026 se descubrió que las fuerzas especiales ucranias operaban desde Libia, donde han establecido una base naval y apoyan militarmente al Gobierno del primer ministro, Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh, en su lucha contra la oposición, sustentada a su vez por Moscú. Las operaciones desde Libia quedaron a la vista cuando desde allí se dispararon los drones que atacaron el metanero ruso Arctic Metagaz, que navegó a la deriva durante días por aguas europeas con el riesgo de provocar una catástrofe ecológica. Más cerca, aún se desconoce si las fuerzas especiales ucranias estuvieron detrás de las explosiones que hundieron el carguero ruso Ursa Major en 2024 frente a la costa de Murcia. El Ursa Major transportaba reactores nucleares.

Ucrania está sometida a una invasión cruel e ilegal que ha destruido sus infraestructuras y ha dejado centenares de miles de muertos, un engranaje puesto en marcha por Rusia y que ha llevado desde hace tiempo a la expansión de la guerra más allá de sus fronteras. Ante esta extensión del campo de batalla, los ucranios tienen derecho a defenderse, y buscan golpear dondequiera que esté el agresor o allí donde se encuentren los medios que le sirven en su esfuerzo bélico. La condición es el respeto de las normas internacionales y la distinción de los objetivos militares y civiles.

En la respuesta militar, Kiev actúa como primera línea de defensa para el resto del continente. Los actos de sabotaje ruso en territorio europeo han aumentado un 16% en el último año, según un informe publicado esta semana. La metralla de la guerra ha llegado en forma de proyectiles a Polonia, a Chipre o a Alemania, y ha elevado la inquietud en una parte de la ciudadanía. En Alemania, donde estos días se está juzgando a un exmilitar ucranio por haber participado en el sabotaje en 2022 del gasoducto Nord Stream, las encuestas señalan por primera vez que hay una mayoría de la sociedad contraria a ayudar a Ucrania: estas operaciones llegan en un momento en el que se acercan al poder partidos que quieren cerrar el grifo de la asistencia militar y económica, y el apoyo de Estados Unidos depende del humor diario de Donald Trump.

Estamos ante una escalada peligrosa que obliga a extremar la vigilancia para evitar la extensión de un conflicto en el que Europa no puede considerarse ajena. Ahora, cuando Trump busca un acuerdo con Vladímir Putin a espaldas de los europeos, no es el momento de rebajar la ayuda a Ucrania. Al contrario. Y precisamente por este motivo, este país debe lograr que el legítimo esfuerzo bélico no acabe erosionando el apoyo de sus aliados.

articles.title: Israeli ‘direct hit ‘on Doctors Without Borders Gaza clinic kills 2 staff
articles.summary: MSF says premises 'clearly marked' with its logos, location communicated to and known by Israeli military.
articles.preview: MSF says premises ‘clearly marked’ with its logos, location communicated to and known by Israeli military. Two staff members of Doctors Without Borders, the humanitarian relief agency known by its French initials MSF, have been killed in an Israeli strike on one of its clinics in Gaza City. “We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” MSF said on X on Friday.
articles.body:
MSF says premises ‘clearly marked’ with its logos, location communicated to and known by Israeli military.

Two staff members of Doctors Without Borders, the humanitarian relief agency known by its French initials MSF, have been killed in an Israeli strike on one of its clinics in Gaza City.

“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” MSF said on X on Friday.

It called the attack a “direct hit” and said the killings bring the number of its staff killed in Gaza to 17.

The agency’s premises were “clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military”, the group said.

It called for those responsible to be held accountable.

In a statement following the strike, the Israeli military claimed, without providing evidence, that the two workers were members of Hamas.

World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the attack “outrageous and unacceptable”.

“Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked,” he wrote on X.

The Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor condemned the “attack on a clearly marked MSF clinic” and accused Israel of “systematic targeting of humanitarian personnel and facilities”.

A pattern of attacks

Israel’s forces have killed more than 1,700 health workers since the start of its genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

In January, MSF said Israel had blocked its supplies and denied entry to all its international staff since the start of the year.

Israeli officials have alleged, without proof, that aid groups are linked to Hamas, while aid organisations say such accusations have helped normalise attacks on humanitarian workers.

Earlier this week, an Israeli strike in Gaza killed Adel al-Helou, who had worked for 35 years for UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees.

Al-Helou was supplying water to residents of the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza. Three other people were wounded in the attack, UNRWA and medics said.

The strike came despite a “ceasefire” that took effect in October 2025, which Israel has repeatedly violated.

Israeli attacks during this period have killed at least 1,705 people, bringing the overall death toll in the war to at least 74,772, according to the Health Ministry in Gaza.

articles.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
articles.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
articles.preview: Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over. articles.body:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Surviving blackouts

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

Raving through the war

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% â way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method â sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia â "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a cafÃ© here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

How does it all end?

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

articles.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
articles.preview: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives. In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin. "Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

- Published20 November

- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

- Published6 days ago

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."

He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.

"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them moreâ¦ It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink â and its military version, Starshield â were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Tough winter

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

He declined to be more specific.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy amid rising fuel costs

November 27, 2026

The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.

Norwegian low-cost, long-haul airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday.

The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy.

Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East.

What did Norse Atlantic say about the bankruptcy filing?

Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.

But the announcement of plans to file for bankruptcy followed fairly soon after.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.

Other companies in the group like the stock market-listed Norse Atlantic ASA parent company and the Norse Atlantic UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said.

"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.

The company said on Thursday that it planned to file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged and had warned: "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."

Founded just five years ago and based in Arendal in Norway, Norse Atlantic had a fleet of 12 planes and serviced a total of 14 destinations. It had recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025, even before the additional economic strains caused by the war in Iran.

Why has the war in Iran put such strain on the aviation industry?

Small and lower-cost airlines are struggling in particular, but the aviation industry in general is facing severe problems amid the strains on global fuel deliveries caused by the conflict in the Gulf.

In early 2026, as the US launched attacks on Iran — soon leading to reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — aviation fuel rapidly spiked, more than doubling in price at its peak.

It rose higher even than in the immediate aftermath of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although it dipped in mid-summer amid hopes of a resolution to the conflict, it rose once again as these faded and a stalemate developed.

This has posed the worst crisis for the industry since the COVID pandemic drastically reduced the volume of air traffic in 2020 and beyond, a much larger issue that many carriers were still struggling to recover from.

articles.title: Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
articles.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could determine the political fortunes of a powerful dynasty. Victims' families hope to see justice.

articles.body:
November 27, 2026

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could determine the political fortunes of a powerful dynasty. Victims' families hope to see justice.

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.

For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.

It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.

Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.

With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.

Why is Duterte on trial?

Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.

During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.

Human rights groups, however, found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.

His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.

"Filipinos were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction; [that] made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even through extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.

After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.

A 'way of governing through killing'

Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defense. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.

"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.

"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country," Johnson said. "These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control."

Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame in the US, told DW.

Former president remains popular

The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.

Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.

His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.

"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it," Arguelles said.

Why was Duterte arrested?

Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.

The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.

For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.

What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.

Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.

The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unraveled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.

Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.

In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.

What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?

The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.

Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.

By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.

Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.

However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University in the Philippines and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.

"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.

For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.

"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.

"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip," she said. "The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice."

articles.summary: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates have warned.

articles.body:
November 27, 2026

War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates have warned.

For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.

In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.

The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly in 2025.

Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the impact of the conflict.

In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband. Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran, said the girl had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.

"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW.

What the figures show

Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 between roughly March 2025 and March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.

The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.

Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.

But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026.

"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.

When marriage becomes an economic calculation

The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.

In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.

Thompson said that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government-backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.

Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Ottawa, Canada, described a similar risk.

When families cannot meet a girl's living costs and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her toward marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.

War and displacement

Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.

Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene on their behalf.

Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.

Few legal safeguards against child marriage

Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below the age of 18.

"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.

Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.

The concerns also extend to the online space. An investigation published by Human Rights Activists in Iran in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted, or whether the war increased them.

What can be done to protect girls?

Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.

"Education alone is not enough," he said. Families also need the means to support their children.

Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.

According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.

articles.title: Algeria condemns 'spillover' of Ukraine war into Libya
articles.summary: Algeria on Thursday condemned what it called the ‘spillover’ of the war in Ukraine into Libya, after Kyiv’s attack on two Russian vessels off eastern Libya. Two Libyan soldiers were killed in Sunday’s drone strikes which sank a Russian warship and targeted a cargo ship in Libyan waters.

articles.body:
Libya

Algeria on Thursday said it opposed the "spillover" of the Ukraine war in Libya after Kyiv carried out a deadly attack on two Russian ships off the eastern city of Benghazi, calling for an end to its neighbour's political divide.

"We do not accept a spillover of the Russia-Ukraine war in our region," said Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf, adding the ship attacks could "only be condemned."

Attaf said Ukraine's drone strikes on Sunday, which killed two Libyan soldiers, also came as "a stark reminder of the urgent need to reach a solution that ends the crisis" in Libya.

"The divide in Libya is deep on all levels," the diplomat said, calling for "an inclusive political process that leads to unified and legitimate institutions... free from foreign dictates."

Libya has been split between a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in the east, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, who has maintained close ties with Russia and the United Arab Emirates.

Attaf said issues in Libya and the Sahel were "interconnected", adding that Algeria's "main source of concern" was foreign interference.

The minister did not name any foreign country interfering in Libya and the Sahel, but Algiers has often accused the UAE of meddling in the region. Algeria severed diplomatic ties with the Gulf country in September after years of tensions.

In an unprecedented move last month, the Algerian parliament also approved deploying Algerian troops to Niger, with the stated aim of "protecting energy installations" near their shared border.

But reports indicated that Algerian troops would be housed in a base in Madama, a desert area closer to southern Libya.

articles.title: A decade after Duterte's drug war, the Philippines confronts its bloody legacy as ICC trial looms
articles.summary: Ten years after Rodrigo Duterte launched his deadly crackdown on drugs, thousands of Filipino families are still seeking justice. As the former president prepares to face trial at the ICC, CNA examines the human cost of his campaign, his enduring political influence and the divisions that continue to shape the Philippines.
articles.preview: Ten years after Rodrigo Duterte launched his deadly crackdown on drugs, thousands of Filipino families are still seeking justice. As the former president prepares to face trial at the ICC, CNA examines the human cost of his campaign, his enduring political influence and the divisions that continue to shape the Philippines.
articles.body:
Ten years after Rodrigo Duterte launched his deadly crackdown on drugs, thousands of Filipino families are still seeking justice. As the former president prepares to face trial at the ICC, CNA examines the human cost of his campaign, his enduring political influence and the divisions that continue to shape the Philippines.

MANILA / THE HAGUE: At De La Salle University in Manila, a brightly painted van stands out on campus.

The words “Stop the killings” are emblazoned across its side. A mural depicts a woman cradling her dead family. Between windows, a huge “X” crosses over a skull and the words “death squad”.

Above the windscreen is a simple message: “Coffee. Stories. Human rights.”

This is no ordinary coffee van.

It is run by Silingan Coffee, a social enterprise that offers employment to families who lost loved ones during former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte's bloody war on drugs.

Beyond serving coffee and pastries, the project provides a space for survivors to share their stories, spread awareness about the killings and keep their pursuit of justice alive.

“This is the Justice Van. It's been to a lot of places,” said Grace Garganta, the brand’s operations head.

“What we really hope for with Silingan is not only to sell coffee. We really need justice. We believe that seeking justice means we can't just be silent.”

Founded in 2021 with a single outlet in Quezon City, Silingan has since expanded to six branches across the Greater Manila Area, providing jobs to members of more than 40 families affected by the drug war.

Many of its employees are mothers, widows and daughters of those killed.

“Here at Silingan, we don't look at your educational background. The only thing we look for is a death certificate and a police report. These are proof that you are a victim or a relative of a victim of the war on drugs,” said Garganta.

“When (customers) learn we're all from families of victims of extrajudicial killings, they're surprised. We don't force anyone to listen to us or believe us. What matters is for us to be heard,” the 34-year-old added.

“(Silingan) doesn't just give us job opportunities. It also gives us dignity.”

LIVING WITH THE SCARS OF THE DRUG WAR

For Garganta, the struggle for justice is deeply personal.

Her father and brother were killed just three weeks after Duterte launched his nationwide anti-drug campaign in 2016.

“My father was killed inside our home. My brother was taken from our home and dumped in a grassy field. They said my father resisted arrest,” she told CNA.

“I was a student and had to stop studying. I had to find a job because I had to feed and support my siblings. But instead of being able to earn a living, I had to lie low.”

Fearing that she too could be targeted, Garganta sought refuge at Baclaran Church in 2017.

“I was afraid of staying outside. I think if I hadn't fled to the church, I would probably be dead too. I'm deeply grateful to the people in the church who really supported me,” she said.

Her experience reflects the fear that gripped many communities during Duterte's crackdown.

Families of those killed often faced not only the loss of their loved ones, but also the stigma of being associated with illegal drugs and the fear of further harassment or violence.

Duterte had repeatedly urged law enforcement officers to take a hard line against suspected drug offenders, including using lethal force when confronted with violent resistance.

Human rights groups condemned the campaign as a war against the poor.

Many of those killed were fathers and sons who were breadwinners, leaving wives, mothers and other relatives to support their families.

At another Silingan Coffee branch at the Monument of Heroes in Quezon City, one mother still struggles with the loss of her son.

He had been earning a living as a tricycle driver when he was shot dead by an unidentified assailant on Christmas Day. He was 21 years old.

“I took on all kinds of honest work to provide for my family so we could survive hardship and get through each day, only for my son’s dreams to be shattered,” she said.

“Instead of being able to help support the family, my son was killed. The person just shot him, then ran off. He was hit in the back of his neck. My son died on Dec 25. We held his wake and we were grieving at Christmas.”

The gunfire also killed his passenger, a 16-year-old neighbour.

When Duterte was arrested last year, she felt that justice might finally be within reach.

“We were relieved, as if a weight was lifted from us. We thought at last we will get our due. I hope we win. We really hope that if (Duterte is found guilty), he will stay in prison,” she said.

For years, families have struggled to secure accountability through the Philippine justice system. Despite attempts to prosecute police officers implicated in drug war killings, convictions have been rare.

In March 2025, Philippine authorities arrested Duterte and transferred the 81-year-old to the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, where he faces trial for crimes against humanity.

Garganta, who works at Silingan Coffee’s justice van, also hopes the international proceedings will deliver answers that have long eluded victims.

“I hope he (Duterte) stays safe and healthy because while he is strong and alive, the trial can continue,” she said. “I don't hope for his death. I hope the trial can proceed swiftly, so that families like us can quickly attain justice.”

A COUNTRY CONFRONTS ITS PAST

Duterte swept to power in 2016 on a promise to eradicate illegal drugs and restore law and order.

What followed was a campaign of bloodshed that shocked the country and drew international condemnation.

Night after night, suspected drug offenders were killed in impoverished neighbourhoods, some by police officers claiming self-defence, and others by masked vigilantes on motorcycles.

The Philippine government puts the death toll at around 6,000, but human rights groups estimate that between 12,000 and 30,000 people were killed.

Away from the bustling streets of Metro Manila, La Loma Cemetery offers a quiet refuge from the noise of the surrounding city. There, an unimposing structure called Dambana ng Paghilom, or Shrine of Healing, stands as a reminder of one of the darkest chapters in recent Philippine history.

With 100 vaults that can hold as many as six urns each, the shrine serves as a final resting place for just a fraction of the thousands who lost their lives during Duterte's crackdown.

Catholic priest Flavie Villanueva led the construction of the memorial to offer a place of dignity for the dead and healing for those left behind.

Through his Program Paghilom initiative, he has supported devastated families and helped survivors cope with grief, rebuild their lives and seek justice.

But even after a decade of working with victims, he continues to grapple with how such violence could have unfolded in a deeply religious country.

“Why did a Catholic country with deep faith and devotion go through this bloody nightmare? Where did we go wrong? How can we make right the bad choices we made in the past?” he asked.

In September this year, Duterte made his first physical pre-trial appearance before the ICC.

The court has found “reasonable grounds” to believe that he is individually responsible as an indirect co-perpetrator of killings between November 2011 and March 2019, covering part of his tenure as mayor of Davao City and the first three years of his presidency.

For the families of those killed, the proceedings offer a long-awaited opportunity for accountability.

But former Filipino ICC judge Raul Pangalangan believes a criminal conviction alone would not be enough to address the damage left behind.

“Of course, a finding of guilt in a criminal case is important ... but that alone won’t suffice. We would have to reach out to victim communities to assure them that those years, when everyone looked the other way, will not happen again,” he said.

Pangalangan now chairs a newly formed independent Truth Commission, which aims to establish a credible record of the violence through testimonies and documentary evidence from victims' families, witnesses and even perpetrators.

Its work seeks to address questions that go beyond who ordered or carried out the killings: how did the violence become possible, and why was it accepted – even celebrated – by sections of society?

THE APPEAL OF A STRONGMAN

Sociologist Filomin Gutierrez said the answer lies partly in long-standing public frustration over crime, inequality and economic progress that has failed to benefit many Filipinos.

Duterte tapped into those grievances by presenting himself as a decisive leader willing to use force to restore order.

“The nostalgia for a strong-arm leader was there, and Duterte spoke the language,” said Gutierrez, a University of the Philippines (UP) professor.

“He had charisma and he was able to usher the drug crisis into the picture and convince everyone that if we get rid of the drug problem, then we get rid of the crime problem.”

She warned that the acceptance of violence as a solution to social problems could have consequences far beyond Duterte's presidency – it could normalise the use of strongman tactics by politicians.

“When you have a leader who advocates and relies on violence as a solution to political, social, economic or whatever problem, then it may not only activate the official channels such as the PNP (national police), but will also activate the dormant violent sources within the community – the ones they call vigilantes, the ones they call death squads,” she said.

Despite his detention in The Hague, Duterte and his family remain widely popular and politically influential.

His daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, is widely regarded as a leading contender for the 2028 presidential election.

Political observers say she has drawn heavily on her father's political appeal and style of governance, often described as “Dutertismo”.

But the ICC proceedings could influence the country's political landscape, said UP political science professor Jean Encinas Franco.

“Filipinos have normalised electing people from political dynasties. It's very easy for them to transfer their support for Rodrigo Duterte to Sara Duterte,” she said.

“(But) if Duterte is convicted, then his opponents or Sara Duterte's opponents in the 2028 elections can actually use it to say: ‘Hey, we were right in the first place’.”

Franco believes Duterte's enduring popularity reflects a conviction among many Filipinos that his drug war made the country safer.

“A large part of the public remained supportive of Duterte and allowed him to do what he did because they firmly believed that it was something that will save them from the so-called dregs in their communities,” she said.

ON TRIAL IN THE HAGUE

More than 11,000km away, in the Netherlands, the man at the centre of the case is being held at an ICC detention facility.

Duterte is awaiting proceedings scheduled to begin on Monday (Nov 30).

He faces allegations relating to 85 murders and two attempted murders linked to his anti-drug campaign. His defence team has told judges he denies the charges.

If convicted of any of three counts of crimes against humanity, Duterte could face life in prison.

The former president's arrest in March 2025 made him the first former Asian leader to be taken into ICC custody.

Since then, court proceedings have become a focal point for both supporters and critics, exposing deep divisions among Filipinos over the former president’s controversial drug war.

Outside the court in The Hague, activists have demanded accountability for those killed, while Duterte's supporters have questioned his transfer to international custody and called for his release.

“It should have been handled first in the Philippines before they sent (the case) here. I feel like they sold the former president here like a piece of meat,” said one supporter.

An activist offered a starkly different perspective.

“We're here reminding people that he's now afforded the right to be faced in court, which a lot of the victims were not able to during the extrajudicial killings and the war on drugs in the Philippines,” she told CNA.

Among those campaigning for accountability are Patricia Enriquez and Fiona Magallanes, who moved from the Philippines to Europe as students.

They are organisers of the Netherlands branch of Duterte Panagutin Europe, a group advocating justice for the killings.

Magallanes said living abroad brings a responsibility to speak up for those who may face greater risks at home.

“I feel a responsibility to use my privilege here, living outside of the Philippines, to continue to speak up,” she said.

“People who speak out – they can be threatened with repression, they can be red-tagged, they can be called all kinds of vitriol and ostracised from their communities. But it’s our responsibility as young Filipinos to continue the fight.”

But Duterte's supporters are equally determined to make their voices heard. Some regularly gather outside the detention facility, hoping their presence will lift his spirits.

“Our continued support and unwavering presence sends a signal directly, not to the judges or detractors, but to the former president himself that the Filipino people will never give up on him,” said Alvin Dave Sarzate, who has been living in the Netherlands for eight years.

“It fuels him and hopefully motivates him to fight through until the very end. Hopefully, one day he will be brought back to the Philippines, where he rightfully belongs.”

A LONG ROAD TO JUSTICE

Inside the courtroom, the case faces substantial legal and logistical challenges.

Questions over Duterte's physical and mental health have surfaced, although independent medical experts have found him fit to stand trial.

The scale of the evidence, covering alleged crimes over eight years, also presents a formidable task for prosecutors and defence lawyers.

Presiding judge Joanna Korner has stressed the need to keep proceedings moving expeditiously.

At a status conference on Oct 13, she questioned the prosecution's proposal to introduce clips from 197 of Duterte's speeches as evidence.

“We’re anxious as far as possible in this case to keep the number of hours to the least possible without making it impossible for you to present your case,” she told the prosecution.

British lawyer Peter Haynes, who took over as Duterte's lead counsel in May, has repeatedly clashed with prosecutors over the volume and organisation of documentary evidence submitted in the case.

“We haven't got the resources to go through 35,000 pages of Rule 77 material to find all the cases in which these things were properly investigated (and) all the cases in which there is no relationship to the war on drugs at all,” he said.

The ICC's acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang said distilling years of investigations and vast amounts of evidence into a focused case is no easy task.

“Everyone wants to be heard, particularly the victims. This translates into a huge number of documents, sometimes thousands of terabytes,” he told CNA.

But he said reaching the trial stage marks a significant milestone, particularly for those who have come forward to testify.

“Going to trial is extremely important … this is the climax of a long process of work which people do not necessarily see … of everyone who has participated in the building of a case, particularly those who took the risk to provide evidence. That is the biggest moment for justice,” he said.

The legal battle is expected to be lengthy, with the proceedings continuing to stir strong emotions among Filipinos both at home and abroad.

Panagutin Netherlands’ Enriquez said the uncertainty surrounding the case has made the months since Duterte's arrest an emotional roller coaster.

But she believes the proceedings offer something beyond a possible verdict: an opportunity to confront the attitudes that allowed the killings to happen.

“(We’ve been) fighting off fake news (and) false information that people understood from the extrajudicial killings – that they thought it was ok to kill people because they are criminals but actually it’s not,” she said.

“Even if this trial might take a long (time), it’s also an avenue for us to open conversations with a lot of people, not just Filipinos, that this is a system that was created and it’s something we can fight together.”

For legal observers, the ICC's credibility will rest on its ability to examine the evidence impartially and deliver a judgment grounded in law.

As the trial approaches, the divide between Duterte's supporters and critics remains as pronounced as ever.

For some, the proceedings represent a long-awaited reckoning with a campaign that devastated thousands of families. For others, they are a test of whether a former president they continue to admire will receive a fair hearing.

And for families still carrying the grief from the loss of their loved ones, the hope is that the search for justice will finally bring answers, and help ensure that such violence is never repeated.

articles.title: Italy says not informed about Ukraine drone strike on Russian ships in Libya
articles.summary: Italy has joined the voices expressing concern about Ukraine’s attack on Russia ships in Libyan waters. Rome was not informed of Sunday’s drone strike, the country’s foreign minister told parliament on Thursday, warning that further military action could jeopardise efforts to reunify Libya.
articles.preview: Italy has joined the voices expressing concern about Ukraine’s attack on Russia ships in Libyan waters. Rome was not informed of Sunday’s drone strike, the country’s foreign minister told parliament on Thursday, warning that further military action could jeopardise efforts to reunify Libya.
articles.body:
Libya

Italy was not informed of the Ukrainian attack on Russian ships in Libya, its foreign minister said in parliament on Thursday.

Antonio Tajani briefed lawmakers after a Ukrainian sea-drone strike in the eastern Libyan port city of Benghazi against a Russian warship and a cargo vessel.

Tajani said he voiced Italy’s concern about a conflict expansion in the Mediterranean region during a phone call with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybil on Tuesday.

“Our support for Kyiv has not prevented us from expressing strong concerns for the recent Ukrainian attack in Libya, a country where we have important economic and strategic interests,” Tajani said.

The minster said Italy shares the concern for the increasing Russian military presence in western Libya, “We share the concern for the growing presence of hostile actors, specifically Russia, a destabilising factor in the region, few hundred kilometers away from our coasts,” Tajani said.

"We did not know about Kyiv’s intention to strike in Libyan territorial waters, in a port even, and we did not agree with this decision.

We are convinced that violating Libya’s sovereignty is a mistake and that it does not help Ukraine’s cause,” he said.

Oil-rich Libya, a former Italian colony, has been mired in chaos since a NATO-backed uprising in 2011 became a civil war that toppled longtime leader Moammar Gadhafi, who was later killed.

For much of the past decade, the country has remained divided between two administrations backed by rival foreign powers.

Libya is strategically important for Italy, linked to the north-African country with direct oil and gas undersea pipelines. Italian oil giant ENI also runs several major fields and terminals in the west of the country.

The internationally recognised government in Tripoli has cultivated ties with Ukraine and its Western allies, partly to support its efforts to stay in power, and to deter the flow of people hoping to reach Europe as migrants. It is backed by an array of loosely allied armed groups and militias.

The strike in Benghazi was not the first time Ukraine used Libya to attack Russian vessels.

In March, Ukrainian sea drones struck and badly damaged a Russian-flagged tanker carrying liquefied natural gas near Maltese waters.

Sunday’s attack, however, is a potentially significant escalation in Ukraine’s attacks on Russian interests overseas.

Further military actions could further destabilise Libya and jeopardise the international efforts to bring unity to the country.

“We ask all parties to refrain from further military actions in Libyan territory and its waters,” Tajani declared.

articles.title: Iran warns on Gulf military presence as South Korea readies expanded naval role
